say: Most Nigerian tailors start with bespoke work. The client brings fabric, you measure, she pays a deposit and collects later. It needs little stock, but your income depends on your hours.
Ready-to-wear can grow beyond your own hands, but your money is tied up in stock until it sells.
Many small brands mix the two: bespoke pays the bills while a small ready-to-wear line builds the brand.
For example, Chiamaka runs a two-machine shop in Owerri. She sews anything that walks in, and is always busy but rarely has savings.
She groups her last 40 orders: 22 women's gowns and skirt suits, 8 men's styles, 6 repairs and 4 bridal pieces.

say: Total cost has three parts. First, direct materials: everything that goes into this one garment.

panel.heading: Three parts of every garment's cost

cards.d: Fabric, lining, interfacing, zip, buttons, thread, hooks for this one garment.
Your hours have a value. 150,000 naira wage over 150 hours is 1,000 naira an hour.
Rent, fuel, electricity, data, needles, machine servicing. Paid monthly, but real.

say: Second, labour, the most forgotten cost. If you want about 150,000 naira as your wage and you sew about 150 hours a month, your rate is 1,000 naira an hour.
A gown that takes 8 hours carries 8,000 naira of labour. If you skip it, you are working for free.

say: Third, overheads. Fuel, shop rent and data are costs of every garment, even though you pay them monthly.

say: Now two words that confuse many tailors. Markup compares profit with cost. Margin compares profit with the selling price.

card.title: Margin and markup on one gown
card.note: Naira prices are approximate. Total is profit.

say: Bisi sells a lined Ankara gown for 40,000 naira. Her total cost is about 30,000.

card.title: Margin and markup on one gown
card.note: Naira prices are approximate. Total is profit.

say: Her profit is 10,000 naira. That is a 33% markup, but a 25% margin.
If she wrongly adds 25% to cost, she charges only 37,500 and her margin falls to 20%. To reach a 25% margin, divide the cost by 0.75.

say: Now safety. The iron alone draws a lot of power, so give it its own socket. Use a stabiliser or surge protector for electric machines.

cards.d: Never overload one socket with the iron and machines. Unplug everything at closing time.
Never run it indoors or near windows. Its carbon monoxide fumes cannot be seen or smelled, and can kill.
Keep fabric, patterns and fuel away from the iron. Keep an extinguisher or sand within reach.

say: Never run a generator indoors, in a passage or near windows. Its exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell, which can kill.

say: Keep fabric and fuel away from heat, and know how to use your fire extinguisher or bucket of sand.
Also change bent needles at once, and keep scissors closed when not in use.

say: Tag each client's fabric with her name, phone, order number and due date, and photograph it. That photo is your proof.
Register your business name on the official CAC portal, never through a stranger promising a certificate in one hour. And keep measurements and phone numbers private.

panel.heading: Your ready-to-trade checklist
items: Fabric tagged and photographed
Iron on its own socket
Generator outside, extinguisher ready
CAC business name started
Order book and receipts ready
Client data kept private

say: To remember. Serve a clear customer. Pay yourself inside the price. Use margin correctly.
Keep deposits for the orders they were paid for, because sales are not profit. And keep your workshop safe.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Know your customer, not just your style
Total cost: materials, labour and overheads
To hit a margin, divide cost by 1 minus margin
Deposits are not yet yours to spend
Generator outside; iron on its own socket
